facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: arXiv publication of CodeGrep retrieval agent
facts.problem: LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch, not patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration.
facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. It uses CATM (Code Agent Trajectory Mining) to mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories, and a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL.

evidence.claim: CodeGrep v3 reduces resolved-instance rounds from 23.0 to 19.6 (-15%) and tokens from 631K to 514K (-19%) while improving resolve rate from 25.8% to 27.0% on SWE-Bench Verified
evidence.condition: on resolved SWE-Bench Verified instances, downstream agent: OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, temperature 0, 100-round max

evidence.claim: Retrieval quality follows a precision threshold: BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades downstream, Jina (0.445) is neutral, CodeGrep v3 (0.677) achieves net efficiency gains
evidence.condition: file-level precision on internal evaluation set, downstream utility threshold

evidence.claim: CodeGrep v3 achieves Fβ mean 0.576 (median 0.714) with precision 0.677 and recall 0.435, producing high-quality retrievals (Fβ≥0.8) on 43.0% of instances vs 7.0% for BM25/Jina
evidence.baseline: BM25: Fβ mean 0.359, Jina: Fβ mean 0.427
evidence.condition: internal evaluation set with CATM-mined labels, β=0.5 emphasizing precision over recall

evidence.claim: Reward design: applying efficiency signal at advantage layer (v2/v3) reduces KL drift to 0.09-0.15 vs 0.31 for reward layer (v1), with v3 stabilizing at 2.1 turns vs v1's 2.6
evidence.condition: GRPO training, KL-to-reference at step 900, mean turns per inference

evidence.claim: Training data from 67,074 open-source OpenHands trajectories using CATM pipeline, yielding 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention)
evidence.condition: CATM mining pipeline with 3-stage filtering

facts.evaluation_context: SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances). Downstream agent: OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024) with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Temperature 0, 100-round maximum. Training: single 8x B200 node with LoRA, optimizer offload, and vLLM-colocated rollout. Early-stop at step 897 of planned 2000 steps. Internal evaluation set uses held-out SWE-Bench instances with CATM-mined labels audited by senior engineers.
facts.limitations: Index construction cost, repository update overhead, and real-world deployment constraints not described in visible evidence. Precision-only evaluation (β=0.5) may mask recall trade-offs; explicit limitations section and comprehensive failure case analysis not visible in supplement. Whether precision threshold transfers to other downstream agents remains open (§7). v1's reward-layer scaling caused 3.4× higher KL drift and required 1.65× more inference turns than v3.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to agent acceleration. CodeGrep demonstrates a clean retrieval-based acceleration approach: training a smaller retrieval agent via RL to reduce redundant Read/Grep operations in larger coding agents. Key insights: (1) RL for tool policies works for code retrieval; (2) efficiency signal belongs at advantage layer, not reward layer; (3) retrievers need high precision (~0.68) to be net-positive for downstream agents; (4) Git-worktree environments enable practical multi-turn agent RL; (5) retrieval utility follows a precision threshold, not linear payoff. This validates precision-first retrieval acceleration without heavy indexing infrastructure.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the explicit limitations and failure cases discussed in the paper?

facts.title: ExpertPlex: A High-Goodput Disaggregated Serving System for MoE LLMs with Adaptive Persistent Kernels
facts.event_hint: ExpertPlex: MoE LLM serving system with hybrid disaggregation-colocation architecture
facts.problem: MoE LLMs have massive weights (95-98% of parameters) and dynamic computation that impede efficient serving. Existing instance-level prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) isolates phases on separate full-model replicas, each spanning tens to hundreds of GPUs, making resource allocation increasingly coarse. Configured prefill-to-decode ratios often mismatch demand. Prefill-decode colocation solutions using Green Context partition each GPU by phase and fix phase resources during a kernel, unable to track resource changes across operations or layerwise variation in routed expert load, causing head-of-line blocking or idle reserved resources.
facts.mechanism: Hybrid disaggregation-colocation architecture that shares massive MoE experts across phases while disaggregating lightweight attention modules. Expert sharing eliminates over 95% of duplicate model weights and multiplexes dynamically sparse computation, while attention disaggregation reduces attention communication cost. Uses (1) Adaptive Persistent Kernels (APK) to schedule dynamic expert computation at tile granularity for efficient, isolated execution; (2) attention-initiated MoE communication to avoid network interference and enable cross-phase communication-computation overlap; (3) a tile-to-cluster model to optimize these mechanisms for maximum goodput.

evidence.claim: Goodput improvement over instance-level prefill-decode disaggregation
evidence.condition: Serving MiniMax-M2.7 on ShareGPT workload with TTFT SLO 1s and TPOT SLO 50ms

evidence.claim: Goodput improvement over prefill-decode colocation
evidence.condition: Serving MiniMax-M2.7 on ShareGPT workload with TTFT SLO 1s and TPOT SLO 50ms

evidence.claim: ExpertPlex goodput on MiniMax-M2.7 ShareGPT
evidence.condition: Joint SLO (TTFT 1s, TPOT 50ms) on H800 cluster

evidence.claim: Expert sharing eliminates duplicate model weights
evidence.condition: Hybrid architecture sharing MoE experts across phases

evidence.claim: Hardware configuration for experiments
evidence.value: NVIDIA H800 GPUs with NVLink and 200 Gbps InfiniBand
evidence.condition: Single-node: 8 H800 GPUs with NVLink; Multi-node: up to 3 machines, each with 8 H800 GPUs connected by eight 200 Gbps InfiniBand NICs

facts.evaluation_context: Evaluated serving two frontier MoE LLMs (MiniMax-M2.7 and GLM-5.1-FP8) on NVIDIA H800 cluster. Compared against SGLang-ChunkedPrefill, SGLang-Colocated, SGLang-PDD (instance-level prefill-decode disaggregation), and SGLang-PDMux (Green Context-based colocation). Workloads sampled from ShareGPT and LooGLE representing short and long requests with Poisson arrival process. Main metric: P90 goodput where 90% of requests meet both TTFT and TPOT SLOs. SLOs: MiniMax-M2.7 ShareGPT (TTFT 1s, TPOT 50ms), MiniMax-M2.7 LooGLE (TTFT 10s, TPOT 100ms), GLM-5.1-FP8 ShareGPT (TTFT 2s, TPOT 100ms), GLM-5.1-FP8 LooGLE (TTFT 20s, TPOT 100ms).
facts.limitations: Supplement provides hardware configuration, baseline systems, and workload SLOs. However, detailed latency distributions, network utilization metrics, and complete experimental traces across all model-workload combinations remain partially visible. PDD baseline for GLM-5.1-FP8 not reported due to 24-GPU memory constraints. Tile-to-cluster model methodology described but full validation results not shown.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to TPN's focus on network awareness of inference stages and KV cache positioning. ExpertPlex introduces attention-initiated one-sided MoE communication that uses mostly disjoint network paths to transfer activations between attention and MoE-side buffers, reducing cross-phase network interference. The architecture enables cross-phase communication-computation overlap. Explicit SLOs for TTFT (1-20s) and TPOT (50-100ms) are defined across workloads. Supplement shows H800 cluster with 200 Gbps InfiniBand network, but explicit network-awareness of inference stages or network utilization metrics remain unclear.

facts.title: The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling
facts.event_hint: Systematic evaluation of programmatic vs JSON tool calling across 14 LLMs on BFCL v4 benchmark
facts.problem: Lack of systematic evaluation comparing programmatic tool calling (tools as code) to native JSON tool calling across model generations under real-world task conditions
facts.mechanism: Programmatic tool calling exposes tools as typed Python stubs that models invoke through executable code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn via subprocess, replacing rigid JSON function-call objects

evidence.claim: 11 of 14 models match or exceed baseline accuracy under programmatic tool calling on BFCL v4 subset
evidence.condition: 309-entry BFCL v4 subset, 8 task categories

evidence.claim: GPT-5.6 family achieves 10.6% absolute improvement over JSON tool calling baseline
Programmatic tool calling achieves 18.8% absolute accuracy gap over JSON tool calling at chain lengths ≥12
evidence.condition: Sequential chaining tasks, 52 entries, chain lengths 2-20

evidence.claim: JSON tool calling drops tool calls above model-specific fan-out threshold (N=70-72 for Claude Sonnet 5); programmatic maintains 100% at N=100
evidence.baseline: JSON tool calling drops calls at N=70-72
evidence.condition: Claude Sonnet 5, parallel fan-out with probe entries at N∈{60,70,72,75,100}

evidence.claim: Under context flooding, programmatic tool calling stable (+5.5%), JSON degrades 2.3%, filesystem-discovery degrades 32%
evidence.condition: Context rot ablation, 31 entries per condition, 128 total schemas (flood vs filtered)

facts.evaluation_context: 309-entry BFCL v4 subset across 8 task categories (simple_python, multiple, parallel, parallel_multiple, live_simple, live_multiple, live_parallel, live_parallel_multiple). 14 models evaluated spanning Anthropic (5 models) and OpenAI (9 models) from November 2024 to July 2026. All experiments at temperature 0. Ablation studies: chaining (n=52, chain lengths 2-20), parallelism (n=32 enumeration entries, fan-out 7-48 plus probes), context rot (n=31 per condition). Deterministic scorer with normalized string comparison. 95% Wilson confidence intervals reported. Per-category accuracy now available (Table 6) showing macro-averaged results across all 14 models.
facts.limitations: Results divide along model generation lines: all Anthropic models and three newest GPT generations match/exceed baseline, while three older GPT models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.4-mini) do not. Small ablation sample sizes (n=31-52) produce wide confidence intervals; only cross-model aggregate patterns treated as reliable. Evaluation limited to representative BFCL v4 subset, not full benchmark. Three OpenAI models exhibit catastrophic \n encoding failures in programmatic tool calling, particularly harmful in chaining and parallel tasks requiring multiline scripts or asyncio.gather. Token consumption evidence limited to single crossover point (N≈26); full cost curves not reported. End-to-end latency not measured. Models frequently produce correct aggregation answers from parametric knowledge without executing enumeration calls, complicating fidelity assessment. Production deployment costs and error recovery not evaluated.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to Agent工具执行链优化. Programmatic tool calling addresses the topic's core question about whether tool calling parallelization introduces correctness risks by demonstrating it matches or exceeds JSON baseline in 13/14 models under fan-out conditions with near-perfect enumeration accuracy. The mechanism (single-turn code execution vs multi-turn JSON calls) may reduce redundant reads and context-building overhead in code agents, but the paper provides minimal empirical data on Read/Grep/tool call counts, token consumption curves, or end-to-end latency—key metrics in the project context. The \n encoding failure mode in older OpenAI models represents a production risk for code agents relying on multiline scripts.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the token consumption and latency differences between programmatic and JSON tool calling paradigms?
What are the error rates and failure modes (syntax errors, runtime errors, hallucinated functions) for programmatic tool calling?
